questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A before and after pair of reports
questions.learningObjective: Explain the value of pairing two dated condition reports.
questions.stem: The editorial note asks why a condition report is more useful in pairs, an earlier one and a later one, than alone.

answer.exemplar: One report describes a moment, so it cannot show whether the object is improving or deteriorating. Paired with an earlier report, the same entries can be compared over time, and a change in flaking, colour or stability becomes visible. A conservator can then judge whether a treatment slowed the damage or only recorded it.

questions.explanation: A single report captures a snapshot and cannot show direction of change. Two dated reports let the same entries be compared, revealing whether a problem is advancing and whether a treatment worked.
questions.hint: Ask what a second date lets the team compare.

questions.hint: Subtract the frame defects from the listed total.

questions.topic: The gap between circle of and after
questions.learningObjective: Explain the distinction between the two workshop labels.
questions.stem: The editors ask how the phrase after his death should be explained to a reader who knows only the word circle.

answer.exemplar: The two labels are distinguished by when the followers worked and by how close their training was to the master. After his death names his former assistants and their imitators, whose connection runs through the workshop rather than through the master's own hand.

questions.explanation: The distinction is temporal: circle of covers those working in the master's presence, after his death those working later from his workshop. Neither attributes the work to the master's own hand.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What infrared reflectography shows
questions.learningObjective: Explain how reflectography reveals a hidden composition.
questions.stem: Two note takers are asked to explain why infrared reflectography can reveal a composition that the finished picture does not show.

answer.exemplar: Infrared reflectography sends light into the paint and records what comes back from the drawing layer beneath it, so lines of the earlier composition appear as darker marks under the visible picture. Where the painter changed his mind, the underdrawing keeps the first idea, and where he repeated a form, the underdrawing confirms the plan rather than the finished effect.

questions.explanation: The method records the layer below the paint, so an abandoned first composition remains legible. What it shows is the drawing, not the finished surface, which is why it differs from what the eye sees.
questions.hint: Ask which layer the method records.

questions.hint: Add the three groups of features together.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The limit of physical evidence
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an examination cannot settle intention.
questions.stem: The note takers are asked why a technical examination cannot settle what an artist intended, and to explain.

answer.exemplar: An examination observes the object as it is: the layers, the colours, the fibres, the structure and the marks of use. Intention is not present in those materials, and any account of it has to be inferred from the choices the maker made. A report may narrow the possible intentions, but it cannot read them off the surface as a laboratory result.

questions.explanation: An examination observes materials and structure, while intention must be inferred from choices. A method can narrow the possible purposes, but it cannot read them off the object as a measurement.
questions.hint: Ask what an examination actually observes.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the gap between the two workshop labels.

answer.exemplar: Circle of names the followers who worked around the master, close enough in time and training that the master's practice shaped their work directly, and the connection can often be argued from dated records. questions.learningObjective: Explain why two imaging methods answer different questions.
questions.stem: Two report readers are asked to explain why an infrared image and a radiograph give different kinds of answer about the same painting.

answer.exemplar: The two methods interrogate the object in different ways. Reflectography sends light into the paint and brings back the drawing beneath, so it reports the plan the painter drew. One shows a decision about the picture, the other shows what the picture is made of.

questions.explanation: Reflectography reports the drawing under the paint, radiography the density of the material. One concerns the maker's decisions, the other the substance of the object, so answers cannot be merged.

questions.topic: A before and after pair of reports
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a pair of reports beats a single report.
questions.stem: The editors are asked why a pair of condition reports is more valuable than either report alone, and to explain.

answer.exemplar: A single report fixes a state of the object at one date and therefore cannot show a direction of change. Two reports at known dates let the same entries be set against one another, and a stable adhesive in 1955 can be compared with a brittle one in 2005. questions.explanation: One report is a snapshot and a snapshot cannot show a direction. Two dated reports make the same entries comparable, and the interval between them measures what changed and what did not.
